title: This Shrimp's Punch Creates a Flash Hotter Than the Sun's Surface
youtube_description:
This shrimp punches like a bullet leaving a gun — and it doesn't even have to hit you to hurt you.

Meet the peacock mantis shrimp: four inches long, with front claws that don't swing so much as fire. They're cocked back like a loaded spring, then released — hitting with about 1,500 newtons of force, accelerating faster than a bullet leaving a rifle barrel. That's roughly ten thousand times the pull of gravity, fast enough to reach about fifty miles an hour underwater.

Here's the part most people don't know: the claw moves so fast it boils a pocket of water behind it. When that bubble collapses, it delivers a second, invisible punch — even if the claw itself misses. For a fraction of a millisecond, that collapse reaches temperatures in the same range as the surface of the sun, in a flash of light called sonoluminescence. Scientists only measured this directly for the first time in February 2025, when a laser experiment at Northwestern confirmed what researchers had predicted a decade earlier.

This channel covers the real, physics-backed biology behind the ocean's strangest creatures — subscribe for more animals that shouldn't be able to do what they do.

Sources: Alderete et al., Science, Feb 2025 (Northwestern University / Institute for Light and Matter). Photography: L. Sawitri, C. Gloor, J. Petersen, C. Robertson (CC BY), Wikimedia Commons.
